title: Spared from Maguindanao massacre: Unnamed journalist’s 17 years of silence
summary: The journalist was flagged down but allowed to leave, in what has been described as a stroke of luck: one of the police officials who stopped the journalist was an acquaintance

blocks.text: MAGUINDANAO DEL SUR, Philippines – For 17 years, a journalist who witnessed the early stages of the infamous Maguindanao massacre has remained silent about what unfolded on the day 58 people were abducted and killed, including 32 journalists and media workers.

The journalist was not among those traveling in the convoy on November 23, 2009. Running late, the media worker was on the way to meet the group along the highway when an armed group flagged down the vehicle.

The journalist was eventually allowed to leave, in what Maguindanao del Sur Representative Esmael “Toto” Mangudadatu described as a stroke of luck: one of the police officials who stopped the journalist was an acquaintance. That police official was later convicted, along with several others, in connection with the massacre.

blocks.caption: REMEMBERING. Families of Maguindanao Massacre victims, including Maguindanao del Sur Representative Toto Mangudadatu gather for a reunion-lunch to commemorate the 17th anniversary of the carnage, in Buluan, Maguindanao del Sur. Ferdinandh Cabrera/Rappler

blocks.text: The convoy the journalist had been trying to meet was carrying Mangudadatu’s wife, sisters, relatives, lawyers, political aides and journalists to the provincial election office to file his certificate of candidacy for governor. Mangudadatu was challenging Andal Ampatuan Jr., son of the incumbent governor and patriarch of one of Mindanao’s most powerful political clans, in the 2010 elections.

The convoy never reached its destination. In Ampatuan town, armed men seized its passengers and killed 58 people, including 32 journalists and media workers. Motorists and other civilians were also caught in the carnage, some mistaken for members of the convoy. One media worker remains missing to this day.

The Maguindanao massacre became one of the deadliest episodes of political violence in Philippine history and one of the world’s worst single attacks on journalists. It exposed the reach of powerful political clans, their armed networks and a culture of impunity in which an electoral challenge could end in mass murder.

Nearly two decades later, Mangudadatu is appealing to the journalist to break the silence, hoping that an account of what was witnessed before the killings could help fill gaps in the history of a day that continues to haunt the victims’ families.

Speaking at a gathering marking the massacre’s 17th anniversary in Buluan, Maguindanao del Sur, attended by more than 20 relatives of the slain media workers and members of the Mangudadatu family, the lawmaker said he had long wrestled with whether to disclose the existence of the journalist.
He had considered waiting until the 20th anniversary. But the uncertainty of life, he said, made him think that another three years might be too long to wait.

“I had thought of waiting until two decades, but then I realized that maybe my life wouldn’t reach that far, or maybe theirs wouldn’t either,” Mangudadatu said in Filipino, appealing directly to the unnamed journalist.
He declined to disclose the journalist’s identity or whether the media worker remained in the profession.
Mangudadatu said there were details of what happened that day known only to him and the journalist, details that had never been publicly discussed in the 17 years since the killings.
He recalled that whenever their paths crossed, including at a recent event in Cotabato City, both would fall silent, their eyes cast down, weighed by the memory of what happened.
For Mangudadatu, what the journalist saw could help fill gaps in the public account of the massacre while easing the burden of a painful memory carried for almost two decades.
“What we are fighting for here is not just one life, but many lives,” he said. “We are fighting for justice so that what happened will never happen again.”
Among those who gathered on November 23 was 17-year-old Franzitha Subang, now a senior high school student whose parents were both killed in the massacre.

Her father, Ian “Joker” Subang, was publisher for Socsargen Today, a small community newspaper based in General Santos City. Her mother, Eleanor “Lea” Dalmacio, was a reporter for the same publication.

Less than a month old when the killings took place, Franzitha learned about the massacre through accounts shared by her guardians and news reports. Seventeen years later, she said the pain remained, but her immediate concern was her future, particularly her education, as scholarships previously offered to victims’ families had ended.

“It’s so hard for me and my other siblings to continue our studies since there are no more scholarships, just like what happened with my older sibling,” said Franzitha, the third of her parents’ children, who was adopted and raised by her aunt.

Reflecting on the case as a senior high school student, she said: “What I learned in this life is that if you are powerful, you can easily get justice, but for us who are poor, it is next to impossible.”

Although key figures, including former regional governor Zaldy Ampatuan of the now-defunct Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) and former Datu Unsay mayor Andal Ampatuan Jr., were convicted of murder in December 2019, the victims’ families, media groups and legal advocates continue to seek full accountability, the arrest of several dozen others still at large, and the resolution of pending appeals and payment of civil damages.
Supreme Court Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda on Monday, November 23, urged the Court of Appeals to swiftly resolve pending appeals in the massacre case.

Speaking at his first flag-raising ceremony as chief justice, held on the 17th anniversary of the killings, Zalameda called for prompt action while upholding due process and the rights of all parties.
Pending before the appeals court are challenges by convicted members of the Ampatuan clan to the 2019 regional court verdict, as well as petitions involving civil damages for the victims’ heirs.

blocks.caption: Maguindanao massacre victims’ families still await compensation after 16 years

blocks.text: Jergin Dela Cruz, daughter of murdered Saksi News and Mindanao Focus journalist Gina Dela Cruz, said her family had endured immense hardship over the past 17 years. Expressing hope that the appellate court would rule in favor of the victims, she appealed to journalists to continue reporting the truth.
“I appeal to journalists across the entire country to continue and be brave in telling the truth,” she said.

Ronnie Perante Jr., 25, whose father, Ronnie Sr., worked for the Cagayan de Oro-based Gold Star Daily, said the prolonged appeals process raised concerns that the outcome might not favor the victims’ families. He said financial difficulties and the termination of educational assistance had prevented him from completing college.

“The case should have ended long ago,” Perante said in a mix of Filipino and English. “If they were truly in favor of us, it would have been resolved a long time ago. So there is really a lingering fear that the appeals will not go in our favor. The compensation claims would be a big help as we move on.”
Mangudadatu said the anniversary served as a reminder of the dangers of unchecked political power, even as the province sought to move forward.

“Whenever the Maguindanao massacre is mentioned, let us always remember that it was the gravest example of a leader’s abuse of power – something that must never be emulated,” he said in Filipino, referring to the impunity that led to the killings.
Although the principal perpetrators remain behind bars, Mangudadatu said his family continued to pursue full justice while trying to rebuild their lives.
“Even so, we will not stop searching for full justice. We have also moved on, because it wouldn’t be right if we didn’t, yet we continuously seek justice,” he said.
He urged the public not to hold the entire Ampatuan clan responsible for the crimes committed by its convicted members.

“So that everyone knows: not all Ampatuans are bad,” he said. “Let us not generalize, because sometimes people ask me, ‘How are things? Why are there still Ampatuans around?’ I tell them, ‘Not all Ampatuans are bad.’ There are good Ampatuans. There are young Ampatuans who had nothing to do with what happened.” – Rappler.com
